name: RAG pipeline
description:
Retrieval-augmented generation grounds an LLM in your private corpus: documents are ingested and chunked, embedded into vectors by a batch pipeline, indexed in a vector store, retrieved at query time by a service that assembles context for the LLM, and continuously evaluated so retrieval quality is measured rather than vibed. The unglamorous truth this blueprint encodes: RAG quality is decided in the data engineering, not the model. Chunking strategy, metadata extraction, embedding freshness, and retrieval tuning (hybrid search, reranking, filters) dominate outcomes — teams that treat RAG as a data pipeline with an LLM at the end outperform teams that treat it as an LLM app with a database attached.

Two design decisions deserve the most scrutiny. First, chunking: naive fixed-size splitting is the baseline, but structure-aware chunking (headings, tables, code blocks preserved), chunk overlap, and rich metadata (source, section, permissions, recency) are where retrieval precision is won — and permissions metadata is non-negotiable if the corpus has access controls, because the vector store must filter at query time or the RAG app becomes a data-leak oracle. Second, the eval loop: without a golden question set and retrieval metrics (hit rate, MRR, faithfulness), every chunking or embedding change is a blind bet, and the pipeline will silently regress as the corpus grows.

Operationally this is a living pipeline, not a one-shot index: documents change, so ingestion must detect updates and re-embed incrementally; embedding-model upgrades force full re-indexing (version your embeddings); and cost lives in the embedding batch and LLM calls, both of which caching tames. The retrieval API is a thin, testable service boundary — keep the framework inside it, not smeared through the application.
when_to_use: Choose this when an LLM application must answer from private, changing knowledge — internal docs, support knowledge bases, contracts, codebases — where fine-tuning is the wrong tool (knowledge churns, sources must be cited, access control matters).
It fits as soon as corpus size or freshness rules out stuffing everything into context, and the team can commit to evaluation as a practice.
Users ask questions your documents can answer but keyword search cannot.
when_not_to_use: Skip RAG when the corpus is small and stable enough for long-context prompting — retrieval infrastructure for a hundred pages is overengineering.
It does not fix reasoning or style problems (that is prompting/fine-tuning territory), and it cannot compensate for a corpus that is wrong or contradictory — garbage retrieved is garbage generated.
If answers must be exact database facts, text-to-SQL over governed marts beats semantic search over prose.

hot_spots.title: Chunking quality
hot_spots.detail: Bad chunk boundaries retrieve fragments that make answers confidently wrong.

hot_spots.title: Index freshness
hot_spots.detail: Stale embeddings answer from documents that no longer exist.

hot_spots.title: Retrieval relevance
hot_spots.detail: Top-k misses bury the right context and hallucinations fill the gap.

hot_spots.title: Evaluation blind spots
hot_spots.detail: Without golden question sets, quality regressions ship unnoticed.

stages.name: Document landing
stages.role: Raw document snapshots — re-chunk and re-embed without re-crawling sources
stages.rationale: Cheap immutable object storage as the landing layer decouples ingestion from processing: replays, backfills, and audits read the raw dump instead of re-extracting from sources.

stages.name: Ingest/chunk
stages.role: Parse heterogeneous documents, split into retrieval-sized chunks with structure and metadata preserved — the doc's 'custom+LlamaIndex': expect real custom code around the framework
stages.rationale: LlamaIndex is the most retrieval-focused of the frameworks — its document loaders, structure-aware node parsers, and metadata extractors cover the 80% of ingestion that is standard, which is why it edges out LangChain (broader agent/orchestration scope, heavier abstraction) for this stage specifically; Haystack is the production-lean third option with clean pipeline semantics. But the doc says 'custom' first for a reason: real corpora have proprietary formats, tables, permission models, and update-detection needs no framework handles out of the box — plan for the framework to be scaffolding around your own parsing and chunking logic, not a turnkey ingester. Preserve document structure and attach permissions/source/recency metadata at this stage; nothing downstream can add what chunking threw away.

stages.name: Embed
stages.role: Batch pipeline computing embeddings for new and changed chunks — an orchestrated job calling an embedding model, not a corpus product itself
stages.rationale: The doc's 'batch pipeline' is an orchestration problem: detect changed chunks, batch them against an embedding model API (or self-hosted model), handle rate limits and retries, write vectors with version tags — Dagster's asset model fits this incremental-materialization shape naturally, and Airflow does the same job if it is already your orchestrator. Ray earns the slot when embedding self-hosted models at scale, parallelizing GPU inference across a corpus; Spark when embedding rides along an existing large-scale document-processing pipeline. Two disciplines matter more than the tool: incremental re-embedding keyed on content hashes (full re-runs get expensive fast), and embedding-model versioning — vectors from different models are incomparable, so an upgrade means a full, planned re-index.

stages.name: Vector store
stages.role: Index embeddings for low-latency similarity search with metadata filtering and hybrid retrieval
stages.rationale: Qdrant hits the sweet spot: strong filtered-search performance (critical, since permission and metadata filters run on every real query), hybrid dense+sparse retrieval, quantization for cost control, and simple single-binary operations with a managed cloud available. pgvector is the deliberately boring alternative that wins more often than vendors admit — if corpus size is under a few million chunks and Postgres is already in the stack, one less system beats better ANN benchmarks. Weaviate brings built-in hybrid search and a module ecosystem; Milvus scales furthest for billion-vector estates at real operational cost; Pinecone is the zero-ops managed pick at a premium. Benchmark with your filters applied — filtered ANN performance varies wildly and unfiltered benchmarks are marketing.

stages.name: Retrieval API
stages.role: Query-time service: embed the query, retrieve and rerank chunks, enforce permissions, assemble LLM context — a thin service you build; no corpus product owns this seat
stages.rationale: This is your own service (FastAPI-style, matching the rest of your stack) and keeping it a thin, explicit boundary is the architectural point: query embedding, hybrid retrieval, reranking, permission filtering, and context assembly behind one testable interface — so the vector store, embedding model, or framework can each be swapped without touching the application. LlamaIndex/LangChain/Haystack are useful inside the service for retriever and reranker plumbing, but resist letting a framework's abstractions become the API surface; framework churn is high and your contract should outlive it. Reranking (a cross-encoder over the top-k) is the single highest-leverage addition once basic retrieval works — cheap, and routinely worth more than embedding-model upgrades.

stages.name: Eval loop
stages.role: Continuously measure retrieval and answer quality against golden sets; gate pipeline changes — dedicated RAG-eval tools (Ragas, LangSmith, Braintrust) have no corpus entry, so the nearest real slug is the experiment tracker
stages.rationale: The eval loop is what separates a RAG system from a RAG demo: a golden set of question-answer-source triples, retrieval metrics (hit rate, MRR, precision@k) and generation metrics (faithfulness, relevance — typically LLM-judged), run in CI so chunking and model changes are gated on evidence. The category leaders (Ragas for metrics, LangSmith/Braintrust for tracing and eval platforms) lack corpus entries; MLflow is the closest real slug — its evaluation and tracing features track eval runs and artifacts credibly, and W&B plays the same role. DSPy reframes the loop as optimization, tuning prompts and retrieval against your metric automatically. Whatever the tooling, build the golden set in week one and grow it from real user queries — it is the most valuable artifact this pipeline produces.
